sections.title: Tutorial: Set up automatic checks for a small web app

parts.heading: Introduction
parts.content: Synthetic training artifact — non-production. Tutorial: Set up automatic checks for a small web app. In about thirty minutes you will create a workflow that runs your tests and your linter every time someone opens a pull request. This is often called continuous integration, or CI. You need a repository on a hosting service, Node 20 installed on your computer, and a project that already has a test command and a lint command in package.json. If you do not have a project, you can use the sample app linked at the end. You do not need to know anything about servers.

parts.heading: Step 1: Create the workflow file
parts.content: Create a folder called .ci in the root of the repository and add a file named checks.yml. A workflow file describes when the checks run and what they do. First, set the trigger: run the workflow on every pull request and on every push to the main branch. Second, choose a machine image; the tutorial uses the latest Linux image because it is the fastest and the cheapest. Third, give the workflow a name that people can read, such as Checks, because this name appears in the pull request.

parts.heading: Step 2: Add the checks
parts.content: Add four steps in this order. First, check out the code so that the machine has your files. Second, install Node 20 with the setup step, and turn on the dependency cache so that later runs are faster. Third, run npm ci to install the exact versions from the lock file; do not use npm install here, because it can change the lock file. Fourth, run npm run lint and then npm test. If any step fails, the workflow stops and the pull request shows a red mark.

parts.heading: Step 3: Handle secrets safely
parts.content: Some tests need a token, for example for a test database. Never write a token in the workflow file or in the repository. Open the repository settings, find the section for secrets and add a secret named TEST_DB_TOKEN. In the workflow, read it as an environment variable. Remember that pull requests from forks do not receive secrets, so tests that need a token will fail for outside contributors. Mark such tests as optional or use a fake service for them.

parts.heading: Step 4: Protect the main branch
parts.content: After the first successful run, open the branch settings and require the Checks workflow to pass before a pull request can be merged. Also require at least one review. This stops broken code from reaching the main branch. Be careful with the rule for administrators: if you also apply the rule to administrators, nobody can bypass a failing check in an emergency, which may be too strict for a small team. Decide this together with your team.

parts.heading: Troubleshooting and next steps
parts.content: If the workflow does not start, check that the folder name and the trigger are correct. If npm ci fails with a lock file error, run npm install on your computer and commit the updated lock file. If the checks are slow, look at the cache step first. When the basic workflow is stable, you can add a build step, a test coverage report or a deployment to a preview site. Add one thing at a time, and keep the total run time under ten minutes.

skim.question: What will you build in this tutorial?
options: A workflow that runs tests on pull requests
A new web application for the team right now
A database server at work
correctAnswer: A workflow that runs tests on pull requests
skim.explanation: Phần giới thiệu mô tả mục tiêu.

exercise.question: When should the workflow run?
options: On pull requests and pushes to main
Only once a week
Only when an admin asks for the team
correctAnswer: On pull requests and pushes to main
exercise.explanation: Bước 1 nêu điều kiện kích hoạt.

exercise.question: Why use npm ci instead of npm install?
options: It installs exact versions from the lock file
It is shorter to type for the team right now
It skips the tests
correctAnswer: It installs exact versions from the lock file

exercise.question: Where should a test token be stored?
options: In the repository secrets settings
In the workflow file for the team right now
In the README at work

exercise.question: What does branch protection require?
options: A passing Checks workflow and a review
Only a review at work
Nothing before merging for the team right now
correctAnswer: A passing Checks workflow and a review
exercise.explanation: Bước 4 nêu các điều kiện merge.

exercise.question: What should you do if npm ci shows a lock file error?
options: Run npm install and commit the lock file
Delete the workflow file for the team right now
Turn off the cache at work
correctAnswer: Run npm install and commit the lock file
exercise.explanation: Phần xử lý sự cố nêu cách sửa.

performanceTask.baselinePrompt: Đọc đoạn tutorial ngắn rồi viết tóm tắt bằng tiếng Anh (60 đến 110 từ): các bước theo thứ tự và một rủi ro cần chú ý. Chưa xem bài mẫu.
performanceTask.performancePrompt: Write a summary of the tutorial in English, 60 to 110 words: the steps in order and one risk to watch for.
performanceTask.modelResponse: Summary of the CI tutorial. First, create a workflow file that runs on every pull request and every push to main. Then add four steps: check out the code, install Node 20 with the cache, run npm ci, and run the lint and test commands. After that, store test tokens in the repository secrets, never in the file. Finally, protect the main branch so that the Checks workflow and one review are required. One risk: pull requests from forks do not receive secrets, so token tests will fail for outside contributors.
